chunks: Best conductor material for PCB layers. The question: What material would I want for conduction layers?
Traces are the thin metal paths on a circuit board that carry current between parts.
The best metal for them is copper, because it conducts almost as well as silver, costs far less, and is easy to etch, plate and solder.
The metal and the trace size set how much current a trace can carry and how hot it gets.
Think of a water pipe. A wide pipe carries more water with less effort than a narrow one.
A trace is a flat pipe for current: wider and thicker means less resistance and more current before it heats up.
The analogy breaks on one point: a trace's heat comes from the current pushing through the metal's resistance, and a pipe has nothing like that.
Resistivity of candidate metals (shorter is better). Copper (highlighted) is within 6% of silver; gold and aluminium are about 1.
5 times worse; nickel and tin are many times worse, which is why they are used only as thin layers (barrier, solder), not as conductors.
Resistivity: how strongly a material resists current, whatever its shape ("What resistance is", "What resistance depends on").
Copper weight (oz): foil thickness named by weight per area. 1 oz is about 0. 035 mm thick. Sheet resistance: the resistance of one square patch of foil, any size of square.
For 1 oz copper it is about 0. 49 milliohms (thousandths of an ohm). Temperature rise: how many degrees a trace heats above its surroundings when carrying current.
Etching and plating: the processes that carve traces out of foil and build up copper inside holes.
Take a 1 oz copper trace 1 mm wide and 100 mm long. You can cut it into 100 squares of 1 mm by 1 mm, so its resistance is 100 times 0. 49 milliohms = 49 milliohms.
Carry 2 amps and it drops 2 times 0. 049 equals 0. 098 volts, about 0. 1 volts. The page's sizing formula says 3 amps needs a 1 oz trace about 1.
37 mm wide for a 10 degrees Celsius rise. That is the whole idea.
"Copper, almost always. It has the second-lowest resistivity of any practical metal, about 1. 7 times ten to the minus eight ohm-metres, close to silver but vastly cheaper.
It's ductile, easy to etch and to electroplate, solders well and conducts heat. Standard foil is 35 microns, one ounce.
Silver is costly and tarnishes, gold is worse and very expensive so it's only a thin finish, and aluminium is hard to solder and plate.
So copper for traces, with the width set by the current."
